title: The Smiling Portrait
premise: Hospice nurse Wendell Winterbourne has always heard the dying count backwards, a private horror he manages with rituals of light and locked doors. When every photograph in his late grandmother's house begins showing an extra empty chair, he realizes the family's old lullaby is an invitation, and something on the other side has finally accepted it. Drawn into the house's deepening unreality, Wendell must recover the song's forbidden last verse from the memories of the dying without singing along himself. In the end he refuses to finish the song, offering his own name to the chair instead, breaking the cycle but losing the part of himself that could ever feel he belonged.
about_author: Theo Dunmore is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who spent a decade in palliative wards across New England before turning to writing. Their fiction explores the quiet bargains people make with death, and the houses that remember.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. On his hospice rounds, three dying patients count backwards in unison, stopping at the same number: seven. Wendell soothes them with routines—lights on, doors counted twice. The beat is dread disguised as competence; his rituals are fraying at the edges.

chapters.title: Grandmother's House, Empty
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He returns to sort his grandmother's belongings after her funeral and finds her room untouched, a music box wound tight though no one has visited in weeks. He winds it down and hears, beneath the lullaby, a second voice humming. Emotional beat: grief curdling into unease.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Going through family albums, he notices every photograph—spanning sixty years—now includes an empty wooden chair that wasn't there before. Old photos, new photos, even pictures taken in other houses. Beat: the past itself has been edited, and he alone remembers otherwise.

chapters.title: Doors Counted Twice
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Back home, his own apartment begins betraying him: eleven doors where there were six, hallways that loop. He counts them aloud and the counting answers back, one voice behind his own. Beat: his protective rituals have become a summons.

chapters.title: What the Dying Know
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, with patient Marisol's fragmented dialogue. A lucid dying woman recognizes the lullaby when he hums it absently and begs him never to sing the last verse, calling it 'the seat-finder.' She dies mid-warning, counting backwards. Beat: first concrete rule established.

chapters.title: Family Lore
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He calls his estranged aunt Corinne, who laughs too quickly and says the chair has been in the family 'since before the Winterbournes were Winterbournes.' She hangs up when he mentions the last verse. Beat: isolation deepens; the family knows more than they admit.

chapters.title: Seven Nights of Humming
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Each night the music box rewinds itself and hums one line further into the song. On the seventh night it reaches the verse before the last and stops, waiting. The extra chair appears in a photograph of his own bedroom. Beat: countdown pressure begins.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Remembers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: elderly neighbor Ada Voss, who grew up beside grandma's house. She recalls a fire in 1961, a child lost, and a song sung over the ashes to 'give the loss somewhere to sit.' She warns Wendell the chair is never empty—it only looks that way. Beat: mythology surfaces.

chapters.title: Pulled In
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He falls asleep in grandma's armchair and wakes inside the photographs: the house rendered in sepia, corridors of frozen family moments, the wooden chair waiting at the center of every scene. Something sits in it when he isn't looking directly. Beat: threshold crossed; point of no return.

chapters.title: The Gallery of Winters
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV inside the photo-world. He meets echoes of ancestors, all smiling too widely, all humming. They call him 'the next sitter' and show him kindness that feels like being fitted for clothes. Beat: belonging offered as a trap—the theme made flesh.

chapters.title: Corinne's Confession
chapters.summary: Corinne's POV. In the waking world, she visits the house intending to burn it, and instead finds herself unable to leave the parlor, humming against her will. She confesses aloud to the empty room: her brother was meant to be taken in 1974, and she let the song choose Wendell instead. Beat: betrayal revealed.

chapters.title: The Verse in the Ashes
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Guided by Ada's memory-echo inside the photo-world, he reaches the burned nursery of 1961, where the lost child, Elias, keeps the last verse written on smoke. Reading it is safe; speaking it is not. Wendell memorizes it silently. Beat: the goal within reach, cost unclear.

chapters.title: Elias Explains the Rules
chapters.summary: Dialogue-driven chapter, Wendell's POV. Elias, lonely and terrible, explains: the song finds a seat for what was lost, but each finished singing takes a living voice to fill the chair. He doesn't want Wendell dead—he wants him to stay and keep him company forever. Beat: antagonist humanized, stakes clarified.

chapters.title: The Smiling Portrait
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He finds the titular portrait: grandma as a girl, seated in the chair, smiling with Elias's smile. Behind the canvas, layers of painted sitters, each a family member who 'belonged.' He understands the corruption of power: whoever finishes the song gains the house and loses everything else. Beat: thematic climax of ideas.

chapters.title: Counting Forward
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He tries to escape by reversing his rituals—counting doors upward, lights off—but the photo-world counts with him, faster, until the numbers become a chorus. His own reflection begins humming the last verse in his voice. Beat: darkest hour; identity under siege.

chapters.title: Ada's Last Visit
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Dying in her bed, Ada chooses to hum the first verses deliberately, entering the song's edge one last time to reach Wendell. She tells him the verse cannot be destroyed, only unanswered—and that a seat can be refused by someone willing to stand. Beat: mentor's sacrifice delivers the key.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Elias offers him everything: warmth, family, a place where he has always belonged—the thing he has craved his whole lonely life. The chair is comfortable. The smile comes easily to Wendell's face now, unprompted. Beat: temptation at its most seductive; power's corruption internalized.

chapters.title: Singing Along
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He catches himself mid-hum, three lines into the last verse, his mouth moving without permission. He bites through his lip to stop. The whole photo-house goes silent, wounded. Elias's smile finally cracks. Beat: climax ignites; refusal made physical.

chapters.title: The Unfinished Song
chapters.summary: Climax, Wendell's POV. Wendell stands before the chair and speaks the last verse's words without melody—a recitation, not a song—renaming the seat for Elias himself, releasing him rather than replacing him. The house screams, then exhales. The portraits unsmile, one by one. Beat: resolution through subversion of the rule.

chapters.title: Waking With Less
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He wakes in grandma's house at dawn. The chair is gone from every photograph; so, gradually, is his ability to feel at home anywhere—he stands outside his own life like a stranger at a window. Corinne, freed, weeps in the parlor. Beat: victory with real cost.

chapters.title: The Quiet Ward
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, months later. Back at the hospice, the dying no longer count backwards—or perhaps he simply can no longer hear them. He keeps the lights on out of habit, not fear. A new patient hums an unfamiliar tune; Wendell leaves the room before he can learn it. Beat: changed man, vigilance without terror.

chapters.title: One Chair, Empty
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Wendell's POV closing on ambiguity. At a flea market he sees the wooden chair for sale, unclaimed, and walks past it. That night, in his apartment, he counts the doors once—only once—and for the first time the number is right. But in the window's reflection, faintly, he is smiling. Beat: haunting final note—identity forever marked.
